video_title: The Warring Visions of American Power | The Ezra Klein Show
gist: Ezra Klein and Harvard fellow Linda Kinsler argue that American foreign policy is polarizing into two extremes — a Trump-era 'flexible realism' that treats international institutions as forfeited surplus power, and an emerging left position that would subordinate US action to international law even when it blocks moral aims — and that neither can work because the enforcement layer has collapsed. Kinsler's non-obvious read: the US is not killing the ICC by leaving it but by sanctioning its judges into operational paralysis, while China is accruing normative power by participating in the system the US abandoned, and the practical future of international law is reparative (victim funds, damage registers) rather than preventive or punitive. No markets or asset discussion appears in this episode; the signal is geopolitical-regime and US political-coalition risk.

insights.claim: The US is degrading the International Criminal Court not by withdrawal — it was never a member — but by sanctioning sitting ICC judges so they lose access to credit cards and American technology, an operational chokehold rather than a legal one.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: US financial and tech infrastructure is being used as an enforcement weapon against a multilateral court, extending the precedent that dollar-rails and US software access are sanctions instruments applicable even to allied-jurisdiction civil servants.
insights.quote: They can't, you know, use their credit cards. They can't use American technology.

insights.claim: Marco Rubio has framed the ICC as waging war on the United States with 'statutes and compacts' and has publicly committed to taking the court apart brick by brick.
insights.speaker: Marco Rubio (archival clip)
insights.so_what: Explicit sitting-Secretary-of-State hostility to a standing court signals that further sanctions designations on international institutions and their personnel are a live policy tool, not rhetoric.
insights.quote: the ICC and its friends are waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles, but with statutes and compacts and the force of so-called international law

insights.claim: US hostility to the ICC is a recurring bipartisan-era pattern, not a Trump anomaly: the Bush administration nullified the US signature to the Rome Statute and John Bolton pledged to let the court wither and collapse.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Anyone modeling a post-Trump reversal should discount it: US antagonism to the court survives administration change, so ICC-linked legal risk to US and allied personnel stays structurally low.
insights.quote: We will let the IC die on its own. After all, for all intents and purposes, the ICC is already dead to us.

insights.claim: US law already authorizes military invasion of the Hague to extract American personnel detained by the ICC — the so-called Hague Invasion Act — which is the hard ceiling on any American accommodation with the court.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: A statutory commitment to force against the court makes US accession to the ICC a near-zero-probability event under any administration, capping the 'rejoin the institutions' scenario.

insights.claim: Both American parties treat international law as a selectively deployable weapon: Lindsey Graham, no friend of the ICC, championed its arrest warrant for Putin while opposing US membership, and Putin himself routinely accuses America of violating international law.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Read ICC-related political statements as instrumental signaling about the target country, not as evidence of institutional commitment — they carry no information about future US legal alignment.
insights.quote: hypocrisy is the tribute vice pace to virtue

insights.claim: Mamdani's video calling for Netanyahu's arrest in New York is a double-edged move: it publicizes the ICC warrant but also dramatizes the gap between the warrant and the impossibility of executing it, which corrodes belief in international law.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Symbolic enforcement theater by sub-national politicians raises salience without changing outcomes; expect more of it from municipal-level left politicians and treat it as noise for actual legal exposure.
insights.quote: there's a danger because you're also calling attention to the posity of international law of its inability to work

insights.claim: The Democratic party's foreign policy is in open rupture after Biden: the left's charge is that a 'rules-based international order' that permitted Gaza and shielded Israel at the UN was never an order at all.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Foreign-policy is now a live intra-Democratic fault line heading into 2028, meaning arms-transfer policy, Israel aid, and multilateral commitments are contestable rather than settled in the next primary cycle.

insights.claim: The Biden administration's own retreat from its founding doctrine is legible in its language: invocations of the 'rules-based international order' declined over the term and officials became extremely reluctant to say 'war crimes.'
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Rhetorical drift is an early indicator of doctrine abandonment — track official vocabulary frequency as a leading signal of policy change before formal announcements.
insights.quote: We get fewer and fewer invocations of the rules-based international order.

insights.claim: A concrete new left platform position is emerging in which 'international law' itself is the answer to when America uses force — Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, answered a question about military aid and intervention with exactly that phrase.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Watch Senate-level Democratic candidates adopting hard legal-conditionality on arms transfers; if it spreads, US defense-export approvals to allies become a genuine political variable.
insights.quote: international law. I believe we ought to be first among equals to enforce international law.

insights.claim: Kinsler judges the 'just follow the rules' platform insufficient on its own, because the US has already destroyed enough of its credibility in international courts that the rest of the world is on notice it cannot be relied on to keep commitments.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: US treaty and institutional commitments now carry a persistent credibility discount that survives changes of administration — counterparties will price in reversal risk on anything Washington signs.
insights.quote: the ship has sailed and it's it's the extent of the destruction of United States participation in these international courts and institutions has been so grave

insights.claim: The left's fury over Gaza is driven by complicity rather than by scale, which is why Gaza splits the Democratic coalition in a way Russia's invasion of Ukraine does not.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Conflicts where US arms or vetoes are directly implicated generate far more domestic political volatility than equally severe conflicts where they are not — a useful filter for gauging US political risk from any given war.
insights.quote: the difference is there isn't a feeling of complicity in it

insights.claim: What the Democratic base actually wanted during Gaza was not a legal ruling but leadership, and law cannot substitute for it — an adverse ICJ finding would not settle the argument for anyone.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Do not expect a court ruling to defuse the Gaza fight inside American politics; the coalition dispute is moral and will persist regardless of the legal outcome.
insights.quote: what people really wanted, I think, was not law, but leadership.

insights.claim: The deeper split inside the Democratic party is that its members turned out not to share a moral baseline — some saw Gaza as unimaginable, others as ordinary war.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: A values disagreement, not a tactical one, means the rift is not resolvable by messaging or a policy compromise — assume durable factionalism on foreign policy through 2028.
insights.quote: it turned out what some people thought was like unimaginable

insights.claim: The Trump administration's operating belief, stated to Klein directly, is that America held a large stock of surplus power idled by international forums and agreements, and that this power should now be spent unilaterally.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: This is the explicit doctrine behind unilateral actions like the Maduro operation and strikes on Iran — expect continued disregard for multilateral authorization as a baseline planning assumption.
insights.quote: that it was not using because it was tied up in all these international forums and agreements and they were going to use that power and America was going to exercise its will upon the world

insights.claim: The strongest case for international law to a superpower is Ulysses-style self-binding: America's worst recent errors came from an absence of restraint, not an excess of it, and UN authorization requirements would have blocked Iraq and Iran.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Reframes multilateral constraint as risk management for a hegemon rather than as a concession — the mirror-image thesis to the surplus-power doctrine, and the one that predicts fewer costly misadventures.
insights.quote: is actually that it ties it to the mast. That that is not a drawback.

insights.claim: Patrick Porter's 'Machtpolitik' — the corrupt cousin of realism — describes what happens when restraints are blown away and a power stops recognizing its own limits, which is precisely when it starts making the mistakes that cause its demise.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: A reusable model for judging when a state's power projection is turning self-destructive: the tell is loss of self-perceived limits, not aggression per se.
insights.quote: this is the corrupt cousin of realism, right? It's when precisely when the restraints have been blown away, when a a power is no longer cognizant of its own limits, and that's when it really starts to make mistakes.

insights.claim: The famous Thucydides line that the strong do what they will and the weak suffer what they must is systematically misread as a creed of realism when it was written as a warning that unrestrained power destroys the nation wielding it.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Undercuts the intellectual pedigree the current unilateralist camp claims for itself — a rhetorical vulnerability in the doctrine now driving US action.
insights.quote: actually that's a warning that unrestrained power leads to the demise of a of a nation

insights.claim: American foreign-policy visions are now more polarized on the question of how power should be used than at any point in Klein's covering career, with one camp wanting unbound unilateralism and the other wanting subordination beyond even Clinton/Obama/Biden levels.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Higher policy variance across administrations means larger regime shifts on defense, alliances, and sanctions with each election — a widening volatility band for anyone with geopolitical exposure.

insights.claim: Kinsler's counterweight to the international-law-as-restraint argument is domestic: Congress's legislative power is the genuinely powerful restraint mechanism and should be used as such.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Points attention to war-powers and appropriations fights as the realistic venue for constraining US force, rather than international courts.

insights.claim: China is accruing power inside international law rather than outside it, pushing sovereignty as the governing principle and shaping definitions — demonstrating that muscle can be flexed by participation, in the role the United States has vacated.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The contest for the post-American order is being fought in standards bodies, treaty language, and court definitions — a slow-moving but consequential channel of Chinese influence that is easy to miss while watching hard-power metrics.
insights.quote: They are kind of demonstrating how you can flex muscle by participation and not by absence.

insights.claim: Klein disputes that China's sovereignty doctrine is sincere, pointing to Tibet, Taiwan, and Beijing's lack of criticism of Putin's invasion of Ukraine — the doctrine contains a loophole large enough to swallow any border China declares unreal.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Chinese sovereignty rhetoric offers no protective signal for Taiwan; treat it as a legitimating framework for Chinese claims rather than a constraint on Chinese action.

insights.claim: The scholarly convergence Kinsler finds interesting — a Moyn/Bali proposal for the post-American order — is a much thinner regime than liberal internationalism: essentially an anti-war pact restoring the taboo on aggression and conquest rather than rebuilding courts and treaty webs.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The intellectual left's realistic ceiling for a rebuilt order is a minimal non-aggression norm, not restored multilateral enforcement — set expectations accordingly for any Democratic restoration project.
insights.quote: returning to the taboo against the crime of aggression and of conquest, right, which has been totally blown out of the water in recent years

insights.claim: The dismissal of international law as fake is a hegemon's luxury: Kinsler hears 'international law is a joke, it doesn't exist' from American lawyers and generally not from lawyers elsewhere in the world.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: US elite consensus systematically underweights how binding these norms feel to counterparties abroad, creating blind spots in negotiations and in assessing how other states will behave.
insights.quote: that is coming from the position of the hedgeon, right? The position of strength and power. It's not something that you hear in other parts of the world generally speaking.

insights.claim: John Mearsheimer, one of America's most prominent realists, told Kinsler outright that states subscribe to international law when it suits them — a candid statement of the instrumental view now driving policy.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The instrumental view is now openly mainstream among influential strategists, which lowers the cost for any state to defect from norms it finds inconvenient.
insights.quote: of course you know we subscribe to international law when it suits us

insights.claim: International law's own technical standards create legal space for conduct people consider atrocious: the intent requirement for genocide and the 'legitimate military target' qualification are the two exploited loopholes, used worldwide to avoid accountability.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Legal exoneration and moral judgment can diverge completely, so a favorable court ruling will not resolve reputational or political exposure for a state or its backers.

insights.claim: The genocide convention has effectively become a memorial to the Holocaust precisely because it has been nearly unusable — the ICJ has produced only one genocide decision, Bosnia v. Serbia, now the sole precedent for the Israel litigation.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The base rate for genocide convictions is one in the convention's entire history — a hard anchor against expectations of a swift adverse ruling against Israel.
insights.quote: the genocide convention has become a memorial to the Holocaust be precisely because it hasn't been able to be used

insights.claim: The stakes of the Gaza genocide fight are about historical memory rather than punishment: a genocide finding would change what Israel means going forward, which is why the argument is white-hot despite the near-nil chance of enforcement.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Explains why the legal fight persists despite zero enforcement prospects — the payoff being sought is narrative and permanent, not remedial.
insights.quote: If Israel is a country formed out of genocide and then also one of the very few proven guilty of it

insights.claim: A sitting ICJ judge, after enumerating the crimes and violations before him, closed by conceding the institution's structural limit — a rare judicial admission that the remedy lies outside the courtroom.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The institution itself is signaling that political action, not litigation, is where outcomes get determined — a caution against overweighting court timelines in geopolitical forecasts.
insights.quote: the court is just a court. You know, there is a limit to its power.

insights.claim: The unresolved core question of the entire field is enforcement — law without police — and Kinsler treats it as the fundamental question of foreign policy rather than a technical gap.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Any proposal to restore the order that does not solve enforcement is decorative; use this as the screening test for post-Trump foreign-policy platforms.
insights.quote: What is law without the police? What is law without enforcement?

insights.claim: The humanitarian critique has fully inverted since the 1990s: then the complaint was that UN process and Security Council vetoes were too slow to stop Rwanda and Yugoslavia, now humanitarians take refuge in the same rules — and the Kosovo intervention that founded the heroic self-image of international lawyers was itself extra-legal.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Positions on multilateral constraint track whose interests it currently serves rather than principle, so today's alignments should be expected to flip again with circumstances.

insights.claim: Ceasefires have replaced lasting peace settlements as the terminal state of modern conflict — 'ceasefire now' stops violence but explicitly defers the political and moral questions, and ceasefires almost always break down.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Price conflict resolutions as pauses with high recurrence risk rather than endings — relevant to any exposure that reprices on 'peace deal' headlines.
insights.quote: ceasefires almost always break down and it it almost kind of um serves as an excuse for um sidstepping the more difficult political questions

insights.claim: The structural driver of the shift from settlements to interim deals is the end of unipolarity: durable settlements require multiple states signing on to solve the problem, which has become extremely rare.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: A multipolar world mechanically produces more frozen and recurring conflicts, raising the baseline for persistent geopolitical risk premia rather than episodic spikes.

insights.claim: Kinsler expects Ukraine to end — if it ends — in an unjust negotiated peace, with terms already trending favorable to Russia.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: A settlement tilted to Moscow is the base case in informed commentary, which matters for European defense spending trajectories and sanctions-relief expectations.
insights.quote: we're already seeing that the terms are likely to be favorable to Russia

insights.claim: The Trump administration's framing of an end to the Gaza conflict has almost entirely discounted Palestinian sovereignty, paralleling the sovereignty-discounting shape of the Ukraine endgame.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Two simultaneous settlements built on discounted sovereignty would establish that conquest and coercion pay, raising the expected frequency of territorial revisionism elsewhere.

insights.claim: International law has lost its power of moral imagination and been replaced by managerialism, and Kinsler argues the Democratic party would be well served to recapture an affirmative moral vision rather than simply promising to revert to the rules.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Signals where a credible Democratic foreign-policy platform would have to differentiate itself — a rules-restoration message alone is diagnosed as politically inert.
insights.quote: replace them with essentially managerialism

insights.claim: Kinsler's own preferred direction is reparative rather than preventive or punitive international law — noting that the ICC is not only a criminal court but runs a trust fund for victims that pays out in advance of and in parallel to criminal investigations.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The realistic growth channel for international institutions is compensation and claims machinery, not prosecution — where funding and diplomatic energy would actually flow under a sympathetic administration.
insights.quote: how do we make international law material right how do we make these um moral values actually have a difference on people's lives

insights.claim: The concrete, achievable signal a 2029 Democratic president could send is material rather than legal — large funding for the ICC trust fund for victims and making the Ukraine register of damages real — because joining the ICC is hard to imagine for any administration.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Watch appropriations to international claims and reparations mechanisms as the practical tell of a US re-engagement, rather than treaty accession headlines that will not come.

insights.claim: Breakthroughs in international law are historically followed almost immediately by catastrophes that seem to invalidate them — the Hague peace conferences preceded World War I, the Nuremberg Charter was signed just before Nagasaki — so present-day collapse is a recurring phase, not a terminal state.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: A cyclical rather than terminal model of international law argues against pricing the current order's death as permanent; institutional regeneration typically follows the crisis.
insights.quote: these moments of real progress in international law are often followed by uh profound crises

insights.claim: There is clear recognition inside the field that something has to change, with practitioners and scholars actively designing what a new international law would look like — but no consensus on its form, which Kinsler calls the crux of the problem.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: The intellectual groundwork for a successor regime is being laid now; its eventual shape is still open, making this a period where advocacy can still set the terms.

insights.claim: Kinsler explicitly rejects the cynical position that international law has made the world worse, arguing people are better off being able to name a genocide and claim human rights even where those rights go unenforced.
insights.speaker: Linda Kinsler
insights.so_what: Defines the analytically defensible middle: norms have value as vocabulary and legitimacy currency even at zero enforcement, which is how they keep shaping state behavior at the margin.
insights.quote: I think people are better off for being able to name a genocide when it occurs and to claim human rights even in the breach
